analysis.one_liner: Requires large gig companies to withhold income taxes and pay Social Security taxes on contractor pay.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its June 2026 introduction, with no markup or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies with at least $100 million in gross receipts and at least 10,000 independent contractors would have to treat contractor pay like wages: withhold income taxes from each payment and pay the full Social Security and Medicare payroll tax on it, the way they do for employees. Today, big gig platforms like ride-hailing and delivery apps classify their workers as contractors, so no employer payroll tax is paid on that money and workers often face surprise tax bills in April. The bill takes effect for payments after the end of 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig workers, who would have taxes withheld as they earn instead of owing a lump sum at tax time, and who would earn Social Security coverage on that pay. The Social Security system also gains revenue, since employer payroll tax would be paid on contractor earnings that currently go untaxed.

how_it_helps.text: Large companies with $100 million or more in gross receipts that contract with at least 10,000 individuals must treat payments to those contractors as wages for withholding and income tax purposes, and pay payroll tax at twice the normal employer rate so the full Social Security and Medicare tax is covered.
Contractor pay treated as wages counts toward Social Security earnings, so gig workers build benefit credits on money they currently earn as contractors.
The rules apply to the whole corporate group, so companies cannot split into affiliates to stay under the thresholds.

analysis.who_pays: Large gig and marketplace companies, which would pay the employer and employee halves of Social Security and Medicare tax on contractor pay for the first time and run withholding. Contractors themselves would see tax taken out of each payment, and companies could pass costs on through lower pay or higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Covered companies must pay both halves of the Social Security and Medicare tax at a doubled rate on contractor pay, a cost that could show up as lower contractor pay or higher prices for customers.

Because contractor payments are treated as wages for income tax purposes, contractors would have tax withheld from every payment and lose the flexibility and deductions that come with self-employment tax treatment, which can hurt contractors who owed less during the year or rely on business expense write-offs.
Some gig workers chose contractor status for flexibility and could see their arrangements become more employee-like in tax terms without gaining employee benefits like paid leave or health coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most gig workers, withholding and Social Security credits are a genuine gain, since the tax is owed either way and Surprise April bills are a real problem. The costs are real too: platforms would pay a large new payroll tax, and contractors lose self-employment deductions and timing flexibility. The bill is targeted narrowly at very large platforms rather than small employers, which limits the fallout but also leaves the central classification question untouched outside those firms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has not taken it up, so nothing has happened to it yet.

narrative.text: Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Gig Is Up Act in the House on June 2, 2026, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day and has seen no further action, with no markup or floor vote scheduled.
The bill would amend the Internal Revenue Code to require payroll tax withholding on independent contractors of certain large businesses, applying to payments made after December 31, 2026.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Large gig platforms continue to pay no employer payroll tax on contractor earnings while the bill sits without committee action, and gig workers continue to owe their full tax bill at filing time.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote since it was referred on June 2, 2026.

against.name: Gig platforms (ride-hailing and delivery apps)
against.what_they_did: Lobby to preserve independent-contractor classification for their workers, which keeps employer payroll tax off their contractor payments.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Gig platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, and other large contractor networks)
industries.note: These companies currently pay no employer Social Security or Medicare tax on contractor pay; the bill would make them withhold income taxes and pay the full payroll tax on it. Their savings under the current system come out of Social Security revenue and leave workers facing lump-sum tax bills.

Mostly they gain: taxes withheld as they earn and Social Security credits on contractor pay. But they lose self-employment deductions and timing flexibility, and employers could offset costs through lower pay.

analysis.trajectory: With eight Democratic sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action more than a month after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to advance this session. Tax bills start in Ways and Means, and the chair has no scheduled action; it will most likely expire at the end of the Congress unless it picks up bipartisan support.
